en: The Chapter on the Three Jewels from the "Chapter on the Clarification of Dharmas" within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Volume One.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Fazang of Xisi Temple in the Wei Kingdom.
The Chapter on the Three Jewels: The Chapter on Saṃsāra.
Chapter on the Triple Gem: The meaning of the Triple Gem is briefly set forth in eight sections.
First, the establishment [of the Triple Gem];
second, the explanation of its names.
Third, the essential nature;
fourth, the manifestation and inclusive integration; fifth, the categories.
Sixth, distinguishing that to which one returns;
seventh, clarifying the functional activity; eighth, elucidating the sequence.
First, regarding the clarification of the intended meaning, there are seven types.
First, it is for the purpose of overturning heterodoxy;
that is, it overturns the honored teachers of non-Buddhists,
such as Maheśvara and others.
Therefore, the Jewel of the Buddha is established.
Second, in order to overturn the heterodox treatises of non-Buddhists and the like,
the Jewel of the Dharma is established.
Third, it is established as the Jewel of the Sangha in order to counteract the heterodox assemblies and the like.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
One who takes refuge in the Buddha is a true upāsaka;
he shall never again take refuge in other devas.
Those who take refuge in the Dharma abandon all killing and shall never again take refuge in the scriptures of non-Buddhist paths.
Those who take refuge in the Saṃgha...
First, one does not seek among the various non-Buddhist paths;
second, it is for the removal of illness,
which requires a skilled physician, medicine, and a nurse.
Therefore, all illnesses are completely healed.
The Three Jewels are likewise; thus they neither increase nor decrease.
Third, it is for the purpose of escaping fear.
As a sutra states:
"If one obtains a single leap, it is analogous to a single refuge;
if one obtains three leaps, it is analogous to the three refuges."
Therefore, the Three Jewels, through their compassion, rescue sentient beings from the suffering of birth and death;
thus, one may leap forth from fear.
Fourth, it is for the sake of mindfulness conditioned by birth.
The Jewel of the Buddha is established so that sentient beings may practice mindfulness of the Buddha and seek omniscience;
the Jewel of the Dharma is established so that they may practice mindfulness of the Dharma and seek to realize suchness.
Therefore, the Jewel of the Dharma is established so that one may bring to mind the Sangha and seek entry into the ranks of the Noble Assembly;
thus, the Jewel of the Sangha is established.
Therefore, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states:
"The Three Jewels are taught in order to open up for sentient beings mindfulness of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Fifth, the Three Jewels are established based on three meanings.
First, the Teacher who Tames;
second, the Dharma of the Teacher who Tames;
third, the disciples of the Teacher who Tames.
Therefore, the *Ratnagotravibhāga* states: Question:
Based on what meaning are the Three Jewels established?
The answer is:
The verse says it is because [the Three Jewels] depend upon the disciples who have realized what the Teacher has realized.
The Six [Perfections] establish the Three Jewels by way of the persons belonging to the three vehicles.
The Jewel of the Buddha is established for the sake of those bodhisattvas who belong to the Mahāyāna and seek the enlightenment of a Buddha,
because such persons aspire to become Buddhas.
Because those who are pratyekabuddhas naturally realize the Dharma for themselves, the Jewel of the Dharma is established for them;
because such persons seek only to realize the profound law of dependent origination and do not seek the Buddha or the Sangha, the Jewel of the Sangha is established for śrāvakas.
Because such a person seeks liberation solely by relying on the Sangha and does not seek it through other means,
the Three Jewels are established according to the three faculties.
The Jewel of the Buddha is established for those who have faith and make offerings to the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, as a field of merit;
the Jewel of the Dharma is established for those who have faith and make offerings to the supreme, wondrous Dharma as a field of merit.
Therefore, the Jewel of the Dharma is established.
For those who are the foremost field of merit among the noble assembly and who offer faith and worship,
the Jewel of the Sangha is established.
These three preceding sections are all as explained in the *Ratnagotravibhāga*.
Thus, its verse says: "For the sake of those with faith in the Three Vehicles, for the sake of the three types of offerings, and so forth."
Therefore, the Three Jewels are spoken of.
Regarding the second [section], the explanation of their names, there are two parts.
First, I shall explain the general name.
"Three" is a number, and "jewels" is a metaphorical object; the name is established based on the meaning of the number.
This is an analysis by inclusion of a number (*sāṃkhyā-viśeṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, "jewel" (ratna) carries the meaning of being precious.
According to the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, a jewel possesses six meanings:
first, the meaning of rarity.
Just as worldly treasures are so called because they are difficult to obtain,
and because sentient beings lacking roots of goodness cannot obtain them even after hundreds of thousands of kalpas—
this is the second meaning of "stainless" (vimala).
Just as worldly treasures are pure and free from defilement,
so too are the Three Jewels,
for they are free from all out-flowing (āsrava) phenomena.
The meaning of the three powers is like a precious jewel placed in turbid water,
which causes the water to become clear and pure.
The Three Jewels are likewise;
because they possess meritorious qualities such as the six supernormal powers,
they cause sentient beings to clarify the three turbidities of afflictions, karma, and suffering.
The fourth is the meaning of adornment (*vyūha*):
just as worldly precious jewels can rain down treasures to adorn sentient beings, so too do these [qualities] bring about the perfection of pure faith, wisdom, and so forth.
The Three Jewels are likewise so,
for they adorn the practitioner’s supramundane conduct;
this is the fifth supreme meaning.
Just as worldly precious jewels are the most subtle and exquisite among all things,
so too are the Three Jewels, for they transcend the world.
Sixth is the meaning of immutability:
just as worldly treasures cannot be altered because their substance is genuine.
The Three Jewels are likewise so;
because they have attained the outflow-free dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*),
they cannot be moved by the eight worldly concerns (*aṣṭau lokadharmāḥ*).
The verse in that treatise says:
"A true jewel is rare in the world;
it possesses clarity, purity, and power."
It is able to adorn the world;
it is the supreme, unchanging, and so forth.
As for the subsequent specific names:
"Buddha" is here translated as "The Awakened One.
There are two kinds of awakening.
First is the sense of awakening,
meaning that wisdom-essence illuminates the ultimate truth.
Second is the sense of discernment.
This means that because the wisdom of valid cognition discerns the conventional,
and because it awakens from the sleep of ignorance by detecting the thieves of the afflictions.
The phrase "because self-awakening, awakening others, and the fulfillment of the practice of awakening have been perfected" refers to a provisional person (*prajñapti-pudgala*).
That which possesses awakening is called an "awakened one" (*buddha*);
this is a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound.
*Dharma* is translated here as *fa* (dharma).
There are three meanings of *dharma*:
first, its own essence is called *dharma*.
As it is said: "All phenomena are devoid of other-natures and each abides in its own nature";
this is precisely the departure from conceptual discrimination.
Second, that which corresponds to the mind is called "dharma," such as the dharma-base (dharmāyatana) and the dharma-element (dharmadhātu), and so forth.
Third, that which serves as a rule or standard is called "dharma."
This is because the Dharma possesses a normative standard that opens up understanding for sentient beings;
herein, the latter [of the two] is primarily taken up,
while the former two are also clarified.
*Sangha* is translated here as "the harmonious assembly.
This has two meanings:
first, harmony in principle (*lihe*).
This means that at the time of seeing the principle of the truths (satyadarśana),
although the minds are each distinct, the principle realized is the same; therefore,
these two factors are in harmony.
This means that although four or more persons each act individually, they collectively perform a single *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical act);
therefore, it is called "harmony in action" (*kāryasāmagrī*).
Thus, "Buddha" carries the meaning of awakening and illumination.
"Saṃgha" has the meaning of harmony;
"Dharma" has the meaning of a model or standard.
Both names are established based on their functional meanings.
Furthermore, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states:
"Saṃgha" means "many" in the language of Qin;
it refers to bhikṣus who are together in one place in harmony.
This is called the Saṃgha.
Third, regarding the essential nature:
there are three [categories] of the Triple Gem.
First, the common characteristic;
second, the specific characteristic;
third, the sustaining power.
The beginning and middle [of this section] contain three meanings.
First, regarding the gate of analyzing phenomena according to their meaning:
within the essence of the Buddha, the aspect of awakened illumination is termed the Buddha Jewel.
Thus, the virtues of that Buddha,
in their aspect as the standard and norm, are called the Jewel of the Dharma;
the exhaustion of all faults of contention and strife is called the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
Although these three meanings are distinct, the Buddha’s virtues do not differ;
therefore, they are called "common characteristics" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). This takes the Buddha’s untainted (*anāsrava*) merits as its essence.
This meaning applies to all vehicles, differing only in their depth;
it excludes only the realms of humans and devas, because they do not comprehend it.
Second is the method of synthesizing phenomena from the perspective of principle:
although the characteristics of the Three Jewels are distinct,
they share the same nature, which is the wondrous principle of true emptiness.
Therefore, it is said that they are identical. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"If one can contemplate that the Three Jewels are eternally abiding and identical to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)."
The nature of the self and the Buddha-nature are not distinct;
this takes true emptiness as its essence.
This principle applies throughout all teachings, with the sole exception of those of ordinary beings and the Hinayana.
Third, the gate of the harmonious manifestation according to the meaning of principle:
within the *tathatā* of the mind-nature, non-conceptual original enlightenment is called the Buddha Jewel;
therein reside the functions of the countless inherent meritorious qualities that serve as the standard for practice.
Therefore, it is called the Jewel of the Dharma.
Furthermore, when these virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are in silent harmony and non-dual, it is called the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
Thus, a sutra says:
Within the Buddha-nature, there are already the Dharma and the Sangha.
Furthermore, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra states:
"The Buddha is the Dharma, and the Dharma is the Assembly."
These Three Jewels possess the characteristic of being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), which is identical to the characteristic of space; therefore,
when discussed from the perspective of the meaning of awakening,
they are all collectively termed "Buddha."
In terms of the rules of conduct, there is nothing that is not the Dharma;
in terms of silent resonance and harmonious union, there is nothing that does not embody the meaning of the Saṃgha.
Thus, it is taught that these three cannot be treated as one.
However, since there is no separate essence, how could they be different?
Therefore, it is called "common characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). This principle applies throughout all the teachings.
This concludes the section on the gate of identical essence, excluding the Hīnayāna and the Initial Teaching.
Second, regarding the distinct characteristics:
First, the Jewel of the Buddha is clarified.
If considered from the perspective of what is attained by worldly humans and devas,
it takes the five contaminated aggregates (skandhas) as its essence.
In order to conform with the world, he manifests the body of a black elephant’s foot and the bodies of tree spirits and so forth.
Furthermore, within the Śrāvaka vehicle, schools such as the Abhidharma maintain that there are two Buddhas.
The body of one lifetime refers to the physical form endowed with the marks and signs produced by one's parents;
it is a result of maturation (vipāka), is ethically neutral (avyākṛta), and is not something to be valued.
Therefore, it does not enter the Buddha-jewel.
Second, regarding the dharma-body:
the fivefold qualities constitute the dharma-body.
In this context, only untainted (*anāsrava*) qualities are taken—
that is, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and so forth, following the Path.
The five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as real dharmas constitute the essence of the Buddha Jewel.
Because contaminated merit is not worthy of veneration,
it does not enter into the Buddha-jewel.
Alternatively, if one includes both the contaminated and its retributive characteristics under the name "Buddha," there is no contradiction in principle.
Furthermore, within this school,
a person is designated as a mere conceptual construct upon those real dharmas;
there is no separate, substantial person, just as one might be called "rich" despite being poor.
If, according to schools such as the *Tattvasiddhi*, the qualities of the five aggregates and so forth are subsumed under the Jewel of the Dharma (*dharmaratna*),
then the provisional person (*pudgala*) spoken of separately is the essence of the Jewel of the Buddha (*buddharatna*).
This is because the provisional designation of the practitioner as a teacher is essential for the benefit [of others] within the context of the provisional.
If, among the three vehicles, the Buddha of the three bodies (trikāya) takes one portion of the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) as its essence.
This means that among the unconditioned phenomena, such as *tathatā* (thusness) and *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through discernment), constitute the *dharmakāya*;
the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) constitutes the *nirmāṇakāya*,
because the mind lacks the quality of being transformed.
By means of the untainted and pure eight consciousnesses as the sovereign mind-kings,
the twenty-one mental factors,
and a portion of the non-associated formations.
Together with the characteristics of the provisional entities formed by the dharma-realm of form and so forth,
these constitute the substance of enjoyment from the perspective of the whole;
this is as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts.
This is explained according to the initial stage of the Elementary Teaching (Śākyadeśanā),
which is also the teaching for Śrāvakas who have turned their minds [toward Mahāyāna].
Alternatively, True Suchness (Tathatā) is taken as the Dharmakāya.
Great Samādhi and wisdom constitute the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body),
while form and appearance constitute the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body),
as stated in the Liang translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
Alternatively, the stage of Great Enlightenment may be subsumed under five factors:
namely, the pure dharma-dhātu is taken as the dharma-kāya,
while the mirror-like wisdom and the wisdom of equality constitute the saṃbhoga-kāya.
The wisdom of accomplishing activities constitutes the nirmāṇakāya;
the wisdom of wondrous observation penetrates both bodies.
This is as explained in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*.
These points concern the final teaching of the Initial Vehicle (Śrāvakayāna).
Their meaning should be explained for those who proceed directly;
alternatively, one may hold that only great wisdom constitutes the essence of the three bodies.
As stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the stainless and unimpeded wisdom is the Dharma-body;
the subsequently attained wisdom is the Enjoyment-body;
and the various manifestations of that subsequently attained wisdom are the Transformation-body.
Alternatively, one may take True Suchness alone as the substance of the three bodies,
as is taught within the section on the Three Greatnesses of True Suchness in the *Awakening of Faith*.
Taking the two greats of essence and characteristic as the Dharma-body,
and the great of function as the two [other] bodies—
this is explained according to the Final Teaching (Ultimate Teaching).
Within this context, the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) also possesses a transformation mind (nirmāṇacitta).
For example, Mahākāśyapa observed the Tathāgata’s mind and knew [his thoughts] regarding Ānanda, and so forth.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
The Tathāgata transforms himself into immeasurable forms and types, each of which is made to possess a mind; thus one knows that there is a mind.
However, because he previously taught [the existence of] birth, he conforms to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) discourse.
Alternatively, there is only the single true nature, which is beyond words and transcends thought, constituting the Buddha Jewel;
herein, even the three or two [Jewels] are not differentiated.
This is explained according to the Sudden Teaching.
If one relies on the One Vehicle,
since these two types of ten Buddhas pervade the three worlds,
it is known that they employ all principles and phenomena, as well as persons and dharmas.
Collectively, they constitute the essence of the Buddha-jewel;
furthermore, all are explained in terms of the meaning of awakening (*bodhi*).
If one considers their basis, the Sea-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*) constitutes their essence.
This also subsumes all that is elucidated in the preceding teachings,
as they are all contained therein by virtue of possessing both the general and specific gates.
The rest may be understood by analogy.
As for the essence of the Dharma Jewel:
in the Hīnayāna, it consists of the principle, the practice, and the fruit.
First, the essence of the Dharma of principle consists of the Four Truths, the sixteen aspects,
and so forth. Second, the Small Vehicle’s Tripiṭaka teachings consist of sounds,
names, phrases, and syllables.
The two factors of the sense-sphere of sound and the sense-sphere of mental objects constitute the essence of the teaching;
the third consists of the bodhisattva’s five untainted aggregates.
That is to say, one sees the eight patiences and eight knowledges of the Path of Seeing, which sever the fetters of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
these consist of nine paths of uninterrupted transition and eight paths of liberation, totaling thirty-three moments of mind.
This includes the four fruits of the householder’s life as well as the untainted five aggregates of the pratyekabuddha and so forth.
Although there may be harmony of principle without harmony of practice,
both are nonetheless subsumed within the Dharma-treasure that leads toward the Way;
this is according to the Sarvāstivāda school.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi* and other such texts,
the untainted dharmas of the three vehicles belonging to both householders and renunciants collectively constitute the Dharma Jewel that assists the path.
It is solely because one takes a provisional person to be the Buddha and the Sangha.
That treatise states:
"To have faith that the Buddha possesses all-encompassing wisdom is called 'faith in the Buddha.'"
Because one knows that faith in this true wisdom is called "faith in the Dharma," it is understood.
Fourth, the nirvāṇa attained by the Buddha and the two vehicles is taken as the Jewel of the Resultant Dharma.
Because the body endowed with the marks and signs, as well as the equal wisdom (*samatājñāna*) and so forth,
assist in the accomplishment of untainted wisdom (*anāsravajñāna*),
they are also, by extension, included within the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
Nirvāṇa is not an auxiliary to that [path], because it is the Jewel of the Dharma.
Question: Nirvāṇa is the Truth of Cessation (nirodhasatya), whereas the auxiliaries of the path are the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya).
If the teachings belonging to suffering and its origin were [the only ones], then the single principle of the Dharma Jewel would already encompass them all;
why then rely on the latter three?
Answer: According to the Abhidharma school, there are two gates.
Regarding the first, the condition of destruction (*bhaṅga-pratyaya*): it does not differentiate between the distinct spheres of the Three Jewels;
if one examines this door according to the actual principle, it subsumes everything exhaustively.
Second, regarding the non-disruption of conditions:
it establishes the distinctions of the Three Jewels and so forth;
therefore, within this matter, it is the most supreme in meaning.
The principle for establishing the latter three dharmas is likewise not contradictory.
What is the meaning of this?
It is as there are two kinds of paths.
First is the path of phenomena, which refers to ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and so forth.
Second is the path of principle.
This refers to the path as being like a vehicle following a track;
these four [factors] that penetrate in darkness constitute the aforementioned Truth of the Path.
As for morality and the others, they pertain to the preceding aids to the path (*bodhipakṣa*) in terms of their specific phenomena.
Because the principle and the phenomenon differ,
and because the universal and the particular differ, they are divided into two.
Cessation is likewise of two kinds.
First, there is the cessation of phenomena. Because one causes the categories of afflictions and karma to cease by means of their varying degrees of intensity— superior or inferior—
phenomena are thus ceased due to these distinctions of excellence and deficiency.
They belong to those dharmas that are results.
Second is cessation by principle, namely: exhaustion, cessation, excellence, and transcendence.
These four types of profound penetration correspond to the previously mentioned truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
Furthermore, because they differ in terms of principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*), they are divided into two:
the absence of suffering, self, and so forth, is the principle that is elucidated.
The Teaching (Dharma) is that which expresses [the truth]; from the perspective of its preeminence, it is divided into two.
Question: Since both the Buddha and the Sangha are persons, why not simply establish two jewels—the Person and the Dharma?
Answer: They are divided into two because cause and effect are distinct.
Question: If that is so, since cause and effect also exist within phenomena (*dharma*), why are four jewels not established?
Answer: Because people employ forceful superiority to uphold the Dharma, it is therefore divided into two.
The Dharma does not propagate itself; it relies on those of inferior capacity.
Therefore, they are combined into a single jewel.
Within the Three Vehicles,
one may internally [contemplate] the Four Truths and sixteen aspects.
Furthermore, the principles of the three natures and so forth constitute the Jewel of the Dharma-principle.

Second, the three baskets (Tripitaka) and twelve divisions of the teachings, including the provisional and real dharmas, and that which is transformed by consciousness, [constitute the Jewel of the Dharma-word].

First, [the teaching] takes the Dharma as its essence; second, it takes the various factors of enlightenment and the six perfections as the essence of the practice-dharma; third, it takes the various factors of enlightenment and the six perfections as the essence of the practice-dharma;
fourth, it takes nirvāṇa, bodhi, and so forth as the essence of the fruition-dharma.
Furthermore, these four dharmas are all empty and non-conceptual, as stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
One should know that this is explained according to the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*).
Alternatively, the essence and characteristics of True Suchness (tathatā) constitute the Dharma of Principle;
that which flows forth from the True constitutes the Dharma of Teaching.
[The latter arises] from the internal permeation by the True and by relying upon the pure teaching.
The various activities that arise constitute the dharma of practice (*pratipatti-dharma*);
this practice accords with reality and culminates in the realization of principle as the dharma of fruition (*phala-dharma*).
Therefore, these four meanings revolve around the single True Suchness (*tathatā*).
This is as explained in the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* and other texts.
Question: Within this context, what is the distinction between the dharmas of fruition, the dharmas of the Buddha’s practice, and the Saṃgha?
Answer: From the perspective of the meaning of that which is accomplished by the Tathāgata.
In terms of the Buddha Jewel, they all belong to it;
in terms of the meaning of the training in giving for the various bodhisattvas,
they all belong to the Dharma Jewel.
Within the context of practice, from the perspective of the meaning attained in the higher stages, it is the Sangha Jewel;
from the perspective of the meaning of what is studied in the lower stages, it is the Dharma Jewel.
Although there is a distinction in their meanings and principles, they do not differ in terms of the essence of the Dharma.
It should be understood that this is explained according to the Final Teaching (niṣṭhā-naya).
Alternatively, the ineffable true Dharma is taken as the Jewel of the Dharma,
as stated in this sutra and elsewhere.
It should be understood that this is explained according to the Sudden Teaching (dun-jiao).
If one relies on the One Vehicle (ekayāna),
there are ten dharmas.
This refers to principle and phenomenon, teaching and meaning, cause and effect, person and dharma, as well as understanding and practice—
all of which are explained according to the sense of the "model" (mūla).
They are fully endowed with primary and attendant elements, like the inexhaustible Indra’s net.
As this sutra states, this is based on the words of the distinct teaching (*pṛthag-deśanā*).
If one includes the provisional means (*upāya*),
all the aforementioned teachings are contained therein.
The rest may be understood by analogy.
Regarding the essence of the Saṃgha-ratna:
according to the Abhidharma school within the Hīnayāna, [it is as follows].
There are two kinds of Saṃgha.
First is the Saṃgha worthy of offerings, which extends upward to all Buddhas and downward to ordinary persons and śrāmaṇeras; all these together constitute the Saṃgha.

Therefore, when a donor invites the Sangha according to the order of seniority, they receive the merit of making offerings to the entire Sangha without distinction between high and low; this applies whether two or three individuals are invited to represent the Sangha.
One takes only those among the śrāvakas who have attained the four fruits and the four stages of progress as the Saṃgha;
ordinary monks are not taken [into account] because they lack the virtues of the noble ones and are thus not worthy of taking refuge.
When Pratyekabuddhas appear in the world, there is no harmonious assembly and they do not constitute a Saṃgha.
A Bodhisattva acting alone does not constitute a Saṃgha.
Furthermore, the Buddha, as the Jewel of the Buddha, is also not the Saṃgha.
Furthermore, among the śrāvakas,
only those with the merit of untainted (anāsrava) jewels constitute the essence of the Saṃgha-ratna;
those with outflows (sāsrava) are not worthy of veneration and thus are not considered jewels.
Furthermore, according to that school, the Sangha is twofold:
first, the ultimate Sangha, which refers to the noble ones of the four fruits who have left the household life.
The second is the assembly of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
Within the noble ones (*ārya*), there are three [types].
The body of one lifetime is the retribution of the five aggregates;
the second is the wisdom of equality.
The contaminated (sāsrava) aggregates of morality, concentration,
and so forth are the five aggregates of skillful means (upāya-kuśala).
The three uncontaminated (anāsrava) aggregates are the [remaining] five aggregates.
The first two characteristics are designated as "monks" (*saṃgha*) by convention but do not constitute the true essence of the Jewel;
the latter one alone is the true [essence].
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, the essence of the Saṃgha is the person (*pudgala*) who is conventionally established through untainted [dharmas] (*anāsrava*).
There are still four cases;
namely, there may be one who possesses the virtues of a monk but lacks the dignified deportment of a monk, and so forth, as should be inferred accordingly.
This applies also to Bodhisattvas within the Three Vehicles.
The essence of the Bodhisattva Saṃgha consists of all the outflowing and non-outflowing merits from those who have reached the stage of the Three Worthies up to the level of Equal Enlightenment,
as well as the provisional entities of the five aggregates, such as form and mind.
The merits, both with and without outflows,
accomplished by Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas from the stage of the equipment (sambhāra-avasthā) onwards, up to the state of an Arhat.
The conventional person consisting of the five aggregates constitutes, in its entirety, the essence of the Sangha Jewel.
Furthermore, among those of the three vehicles,
only those who have gone forth and share the same dharma as the monks are taken to be the Sangha Jewel.
Because all lay śrāvakas, bodhisattvas,
as well as those like the rhinoceros-horn pratyekabuddhas,
have all entered into the Dharma-jewel.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, in the "Chapter on Scattering Flowers," states:
"To scatter flowers upon the various bodhisattvas is called making an offering to the Dharma;
to scatter flowers upon the various bhikṣus is called making an offering to the Saṃgha."
It should be understood that this is explained according to the initial stage of the Initial Teaching (Śākyaputrīya-yāna).
Alternatively, it distinguishes the superior from the inferior to clarify the Great and Small Vehicles,
as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
The name "Saṃgha" means harmony.
There are two kinds of harmony:
first, worldly harmony.

The remaining meanings may be understood by themselves.

The Sangha that sustains and maintains [the Dharma] is the most supreme, because it is able to uphold the Buddha-dharma and benefit sentient beings; therefore, it follows [in importance] after the Dharma.
However, because it serves as an object that assists in the accomplishment of the three types of wisdom,
the Buddha-relic is inferior;
whereas a physical image serves merely as an object for generating faith.
If the activities and functions of the One Vehicle and the Three Jewels are all equal,
it is because Samantabhadra and others also exhaustively reach the realm of the Buddha;
such is the nature of the arising and functioning of the Dharma-realm.
Furthermore, regarding the scope of the beneficial functions of the Three Jewels across the various vehicles,
each may be understood by referring to its own respective school.
Regarding the eighth [section], the clarification of the sequence, there are two parts.
First the specific, then the general.
Regarding the first, the Three Jewels of common characteristics:
their three aspects are undifferentiated and have existed primordially from the beginningless past.
There is no sequence of before or after.
Within the distinct characteristics (bipakṣa), there are four gates.
The first concerns the sequence of arising and transformation.
First the Buddha, then the Dharma, and finally the Saṅgha.
This is because the Buddha is the Teacher;
one relies on the Buddha to hear the Dharma, and relies on the Dharma to practice.
This is for the sake of establishing the Saṃgha.
As the Sūtra says:
"At first, beneath the Bodhi tree, he subdued Māra by his power."
Having attained the ambrosial extinction and perfected the path of awakening,
he turned the wheel of Dharma thrice throughout the great trichiliocosm;
that wheel is from the beginning eternally pure.
Devas and humans attained the Way;
this served as the testimony.
Thus, the Three Jewels appeared in the world.
The *Ratnagotravibhāga* also speaks in this same way.
Second, regarding the sequence of entry and realization,
one first encounters the Dharma, then the Buddha, and finally the Saṃgha.
This means that because the Dharma is the teacher of all Buddhas and is able to give birth to the Buddhas,
it is explained first.
Having realized this Dharma, one attains Buddhahood through the Path.
It is only after subsequently ordaining disciples that there is a *saṃgha*.
Question: Before the Buddha had realized the Dharma, was he not called a *saṃgha*?
Answer: It is as when Śākyamuni Buddha had not yet sat beneath the Bodhi tree;
he was not called the Saṃgha because there was no assembly, and thus lacked the characteristics of a Saṃgha and the performance of formal legal acts (dharmakarma).
Third, regarding the sequence of the establishment of the teaching:
first the Buddha, then the Saṃgha,
and finally the Dharma, as in this sutra.
First, the Buddha manifested himself seated upon a precious lion throne;
next, he gathered the assembly of bodhisattvas from the ten directions;
and finally, he was requested to bestow and reveal the dharma-gate.
Fourth, regarding the sequence of practice:
first the Saṃgha, next the Dharma, and finally the Buddha;
this refers to the progression of one's cultivation.
First, one must renounce secular life and enter the monastic order.
Although one has left the household life, it is essential to practice according to the Dharma.
When one's practice is perfected to its ultimate conclusion, one will finally attain Buddhahood.
Regarding the sequence within the maintenance [of the Three Jewels], if one clarifies the order according to the origin of their arising,
then the Buddha Jewel comes first.
First, because King Udayana and others were the initial creators of Buddha images;
second, because after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Kāśyapa and others compiled the Dharma-eye;
and finally, because ordinary monks were ordained to uphold the Buddha-dharma.
They are situated at the rear.
If the One Vehicle and the Three Jewels are all without priority or sequence, it is because,
within the great dependent origination of the dharma-realm, they are so.
Because they manifest simultaneously and are fully complete;
or because they all possess priority and posteriority,
as the primary and its attendants are mutually established.
Because it is presented as the primary example,
this general statement refers to two or three of the Jewels within the Hīnayāna.
The ultimate reality comes first and conventional designation follows.
Within the three vehicles and the three jewels,
the common characteristics come first and the specific characteristics follow.
The Abbot follows behind.
As for the One Vehicle and the Thirteen Treasures,
they may precede or follow, or neither precede nor follow, as previously explained.
The remaining meanings may be understood by analogy.
In the Chapter on Transmigration (*pravṛtti*), the transmigration of arising and ceasing is briefly set forth through ten sections.
The first clarifies contrariety and conformity.
Second, permanence and annihilation;
third, identity and difference;
fourth, existence and non-existence.
5. Arising and ceasing;
6. Before and after;
7. Time periods.
Eight, cause and effect;
nine, truth and falsehood;
ten, the accomplishment of contemplation.
At the beginning, regarding a single phenomenon of conditioned transmigration, it is conceptually divided into two:
namely, the cessation of the preceding moment and the arising of the succeeding moment.
As the Sūtra says:
It is like pressing a seal into clay: when the seal is broken, the impression is formed.
Thus, the breaking of the seal constitutes cessation, while the formation of the impression constitutes arising.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
Due to the five preceding aggregates,
the subsequent aggregates arise in succession;
all such instances constitute the meaning of this process of saṃsāra.
Within this, there are two gates concerning arising and ceasing, and their opposition or conformity:
first the general, then the specific.
Within the general, there are four meanings.
First, the meaning of contradiction:
taking turning away from cessation as arising, and taking exhaustion as cessation;
because they are contradictory, they constitute arising and cessation.
Second, the conformity with meaning:
if the preceding moment of consciousness were not to cease, the succeeding moment would not arise;
it is only through the cessation of the preceding moment that the succeeding moment can arise.
Therefore, it is through mutual conformity that arising and ceasing are established.
Question: If a subsequent thought cannot arise unless the preceding thought has ceased, since two thoughts do not exist simultaneously; [how can there be conformity?]
Once it has ceased, it cannot arise again,
because there is nothing upon which its arising could depend.
As the treatise says:
How can that which has ceased serve as an object of cognition?
Therefore, there is no equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Consequently, once [the preceding moment] has ceased, nothing remains; what then could produce the subsequent one?
Answer: Cessation is of two kinds:
first, cessation through abandonment;
second, momentary cessation.
Since it is not a state of annihilation, it is not the same as non-existence.
Question: If this momentary destruction is not the same as non-existence, it should not be considered "destruction."
Answer: This momentary cessation necessarily induces what follows;
therefore, it is not the same as a non-entity.
If it did not induce what follows, it would not be this [kind of] cessation.
Question: If each moment necessarily induces a subsequent birth, then it would be impossible to enter the mindless meditative attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*) and so forth;
for once [the mind] has ceased, it must necessarily arise immediately thereafter.
Answer: There are two aspects regarding the moment (kṣaṇa).
First, with respect to the dependent evolving consciousnesses, because they are coarse, all arise from their own seeds.
The preceding and succeeding moments of thought are both equal and non-distinct in their proximity and distance as objects of hearing. This is because,
in terms of their basis, the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is subtle.
The preceding and succeeding streams flow on, ceasing and being born again in uninterrupted succession.
Question: If this is so, then what of the final ceasing mind of the two vehicles that have entered into quiescence?
It would follow that they must be reborn;
thus, there would be no nirvāṇa, which would constitute a grave error.
Answer: If one refers to the initial teaching of the Hīnayāna, [this is so].
It may be as you have objected;
for within that school (the Hīnayāna), it is admitted that the two vehicles enter into nirvāṇa and undergo eternal cessation and extinction.
However, this is not the case in the Final Teaching (Niṣṭhā-yāna) and other such systems.
Because those of the two vehicles,
having burned away their bodies of segmented existence, conceive the thought of extinction and enter nirvana,
yet they continue to receive bodies of transformation in other worlds.
Having received the transformation through the Buddha's teaching, they practice the bodhisattva path until they attain buddhahood;
this shall continue until the end of the future, without interruption.
Because there are no sentient beings who act as non-sentient beings,
among the four types of categorical explanations (vyākaraṇa),
regarding that which has ceased, one further generates conceptual discrimination when providing an explanation.
This is explained according to the Hīnayāna.
Question: Since this subtle cessation does not abide of its own accord, how can it possess the power to produce the subsequent moment?
The answer is: because it relies upon *tathatā* and the *tathāgatagarbha*, this arising-and-ceasing is enabled to arise and cease.
As the Sūtra says:
It is because of the Tathāgatagarbha that there arise the mind of birth and extinction, and so forth.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
"Based on the foundation of non-abiding, all dharmas are established."
Therefore, since cessation lacks a true basis, there is nothing upon which arising can depend;
and since arising does not depend on the true, it does not emerge from cessation.
As the *Awakening of Faith* says:
The non-arising and non-ceasing combined with arising and ceasing is called the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
This is precisely the revolution of that which both revolves and does not revolve.
Therefore, they accord with one another to bring about arising and ceasing.
Thirdly, these two must both oppose and accord with one another to achieve arising and ceasing,
because the former two meanings are not mutually exclusive.
If there were no cessation, there would be no arising;
if there were no arising, there would be no turning away from cessation.
Therefore, it is through their extreme opposition that they are ultimately in perfect accord.
This can be understood through reflection.
It is only when there is neither contrariety nor conformity that arising and ceasing can occur,
because the two preceding meanings mutually negate one another.
Non-duality is taken as oneness because it is free from dualistic characteristics and because both the adverse and the favorable are simultaneously extinguished.
Regarding the second, the detailed explanation:
this arising and ceasing are each divided into two.
Within the cessation of the preceding moment, there are two meanings.
First, the sense of disintegration;
second, the sense of inducing the subsequent.
Regarding the arising of the subsequent moment, there are two senses.
First, it is based on the aforementioned meaning;
second, it is contrary to the aforementioned meaning.
This is because disintegration and the arising of what was previously mentioned are utterly contradictory.
This is because the subsequent projection is extremely concordant with the arising and ceasing of the preceding basis,
since the destruction does not differ from the subsequent projection,
and the preceding basis does not differ from its own cessation.
Therefore, it is both contrary and conformable, without any obstruction.
This is because the subsequent [stage] is induced by the destruction and melting of the former, while the latter relies upon the former as its basis for melting.
Arising and ceasing are neither contrary nor conformable.
One may further consider this by means of various categories of propositions, as can be seen.
Second, regarding permanence and annihilation:
This also proceeds from general to specific.
Within the general [explanation], the four phrases show that because [the preceding] ceases first, there is no permanence;
and because [the succeeding] arises later, there is no annihilation.
Both "together" and "not together" should be considered accordingly.
Within the distinct [categories], there are also four permutations,
due to destruction and turning away from what preceded.
Phenomena do not reach phenomena; fundamentally they neither shift nor are they permanent.
Because they draw forth what follows and rely upon what precedes, their positions are never severed.
Their positions flow eternally without interruption.
Because these two preceding meanings are inseparable, non-interruption is itself non-permanence;
it flows eternally without shifting.
This is because there is no duality between non-shifting and shifting, or between shifting and non-shifting.
Because it perishes and opposes subsequent arising,
and because it turns away from the preceding and opposes its own basis,
it is therefore neither eternal nor non-eternal.
It is neither severed nor not severed;
likewise, this dharma of saṃsāra is neither saṃsāric nor non-saṃsāric.
This can be seen by reflecting upon it.
Regarding the third point, identity and difference,
there are likewise two approaches.
Within the preceding general discussion, there are likewise four propositions:
by virtue of the meaning induced from the preceding moment into the subsequent moment,
and the meaning turned away from the preceding moment within the subsequent moment.
This is not a single gate;
it can be understood by reflecting on [the categories of] both together and neither, and so forth.
Within the second [category], there are likewise four.
This means that the preceding and succeeding moments are not one;
each pair is not two, which constitutes their non-difference.
Consider them as both simultaneous and non-simultaneous.
Furthermore, when viewed through mutual interconnection, four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) can likewise be seen.
Therefore, identity and difference are unimpeded; it flows, yet it does not flow.
Fourthly, regarding existence and non-existence, there are also four propositions.
1. The sense of "existence" is the sense of turning away from the preceding meaning within the subsequent moment.
2. The sense of "non-existence" is the sense of cessation and destruction within the preceding moment.
3. The sense of "neither existence nor non-existence" is the sense of depending upon the preceding meaning within the subsequent moment.
Fourth, the sense that the preceding moment can induce the subsequent one;
this is not without meaning.
Fifth, by virtue of these two preceding meanings, there is non-duality.
This is the meaning of their coexistence.
The sixth [alternative] is non-duality by virtue of the latter two meanings;
this is the meaning of their mutual negation.
Seventh, by way of the non-obstruction between existence and cessation.
Combining the preceding six phrases, they constitute a single unobstructed flow of transmigration.
As the Sūtra says:
"All phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing;
this is what I mean by the meaning of 'moment' (kṣaṇa). This is what is being said.
Fifth, regarding arising and ceasing,
there are also two layers within it;
first, there are four propositions.
Arising in succession based on what precedes and follows is the meaning of non-arising,
because it does not arise through its own power.
Leading to what follows is the meaning of non-extinction, because it possesses functional efficacy.
Consider both the simultaneous and the non-simultaneous cases accordingly.
Furthermore, because the preceding thought-moment has ceased, there is no arising;
because the succeeding thought-moment has arisen, there is no cessation.
Contemplate both "together" and "not together.
Regarding the sixth [section], there are two layers in the preceding, succeeding, and middle portions;
first, within the general middle section, there are four propositions.
Because it relies on the preceding [moment] and induces the succeeding one,
two moments of consciousness do not exist as prior and posterior;
because it undergoes destruction and turns away from the preceding one.
The two moments of thought do not exist simultaneously,
because the two aforementioned modes are inseparable;
whether they are simultaneous or not, one should reflect upon this accordingly.
Therefore, it is neither beginning, nor middle, nor end;
yet, because of the grasping at a beginning, middle, and end, one speaks of "cyclic flow" (saṃsāra).
This cyclic flow is itself without cycling.
Within the general discussion of the distinct [teachings], there are four levels of unimpededness (*anāvaraṇa*):
first, explaining simultaneity without impeding sequence;
second, explaining sequence without impeding simultaneity.
Third, without being hindered by the three times, one speaks of the three times.
Fourth, without being hindered by the three times, one speaks of that which is not the three times.
In the sutras, cases such as "an eon entering what is not an eon" and "what is not an eon entering an eon" should be understood accordingly.
Seventh, regarding the temporal period,
there are three parts. First,
concerning the direction [toward rebirth].
Second, [the classification] by way of characteristics;
third, by way of time and phenomena.
Regarding the first, there are four [sections].
First, from front to back gate:
this refers to relying on the cessation of the preceding thought-moment to cause the subsequent thought-moment to arise;
therefore, it transforms from the past into the present by way of dependence.
The present ceases and gives rise to the future;
by means of this gateway, there is a continuous succession of new births without end.
The second is the gate of proceeding from the later toward the former.
This refers to depending on the principle that what was originally non-existent now exists, and having existed, returns to non-existence;
that is, that which is yet to come becomes the present.
The present, manifesting as it ceases, becomes the past;
by means of this gate, there is momentary cessation at every instant without any accumulation.
Thirdly, because the two preceding meanings are inseparable.
It proceeds both forward and backward;
by means of this gateway,
it gives rise to the inexhaustible while remaining unextinguished.
It is extinguished without accumulation, yet there is nothing that does not arise;
contemplate this as being without obstruction or hindrance.
This is because, through the two preceding meanings, all forms are completely subsumed and exhausted.
Neither proceeding forward nor proceeding backward;
by means of this gateway,
there is cessation without accumulation, and yet no cessation.
To give birth while being unborn—
this is called the unimpeded Dharma-gate. Regarding the second,
the mutual accomplishment of characteristics, there are five phrases.
First, this present dharma arises from the future existence and through the cessation of the past;
therefore, the present is constituted by these two time periods.
First, it causes the present to manifest as having no intrinsic nature and to enter into the past and future.
Second, this present dharma, having fallen away, becomes the past;
it induces what follows to function as the future.
Therefore, the two time periods [past and future] are established as being manifested in the present,
which renders the past and future devoid of intrinsic substance;
both enter into the present.
Third, because the two preceding gates are not mutually exclusive,
and because this refers to the sense of their being mutually supportive and efficacious,
they are established as existing across all three time periods.
Fourth, because it is completely eclipsed by the two preceding meanings.
This refers to the sense that, due to mutual dependence, there is no independent power;
thus, the three times are all dissolved.
The fifth point combines with the preceding four meanings because they share the same principle;
therein, existence and non-existence are unimpeded, and principle and phenomena are mutually integrated—
this can be seen through reflection.
Regarding the Dharma of the third period,
there are likewise five gates within it.
First, the Dharma turns without flowing.
That is to say, based on the preceding cessation, the subsequent arises;
this arising and ceasing, in turn, induces the subsequent.
This is the progression of phenomena.
However, the past does not reach the present,
and the present does not reach the future;
these times do not flow.
This means that while time is characterized by moment-to-moment interruption,
phenomena are characterized by continuity and constant flow;
thus, while the two phenomena do not change, time passes.
That is to say, it is through the passing away of the past that the present comes to be;
the falling away of the present can induce the future.
Thus, moment by moment throughout the three periods of time, there is no interruption.
This is the transition of time.
Past phenomena do not come to the present;
present phenomena do not go to the future.
Because each abides in its own position and does not reach the other,
this dharma does not transmigrate.
This refers to the fact that, fundamentally, dharmas do not reach one another.
"Approximately" means that there is no interval between every moment of thought.
"The three all shift together" is because time does not exist apart from phenomena.
Therefore, because the dharma that flows through time evolves without duality,
it has never ceased for even a moment since beginningless time.
Fourth, as for "non-transmigration":
Because that which does not flow and that which does not turn are non-dual,
there has never been any shifting or movement since beginningless time.
This fifth point combines with the preceding four phrases because they are inseparable.
From beginningless time, it has flowed without moving and shifted without changing;
being unobstructed and unimpeded is the very essence of this dharma.
This can be seen through reflection.
The eighth cause also has four stages within the section on causes and fruits.
One is non-dual existence;
three are simultaneous, and four are extinguished.
Regarding the first and the beginning, this refers to this single thought-moment of dharmas.
Since the preceding cause has already ceased, for whom can it be called an effect?
Since the subsequent effect has not yet arisen, for whom can it be called a cause?
One should reflect that things do not abide, being neither cause nor effect.
Regarding the second point, the provisional existence of cause and effect:
as the treatise says,
"One observes that present phenomena possess the function of projecting [results] in the future."
The present cause is spoken of in contrast to the provisionally established future fruit;
one observes that present phenomena possess the characteristics of being a retribution for what preceded them.
The prior cause is provisionally established in contrast to the present effect; thus,
cause and effect are not non-existent.
Regarding the three being simultaneous:
it is a cause because it has the sense of projecting what follows;
it is a fruit because it has the sense of recompensing what preceded.
It is not a cause because its nature is that of disintegration;
it is not an effect because it turns away from what preceded it;
and because the subsequent [moment] does not differ from the disintegration that induced it.
It is both a cause and not a cause,
because it is non-different from what preceded it while yet turning away from it;
it is both an effect and not an effect.
Because these four meanings combine to form a single process of phenomenal evolution,
they encompass both the meanings of existence and non-existence.
As for the simultaneous cessation of all four:
Because its destruction does not differ from it in inducing what follows,
it is neither a cause nor a non-cause;
because it does not differ from what preceded it in responding to that which preceded it, it is contrary to the former.
It is neither effect nor non-effect,
because these two aspects are not distinct from one another;
it is neither cause-and-effect nor non-cause-and-effect.
Furthermore, if cause and effect existed prior [to their arising], one could speak of them in relation to one another;
however, since cause and effect do not exist in themselves beforehand, they do not exist now either.
It cannot be established as cause and effect;
reflect on this.
Within the ninth [section] on truth and falsehood, there are likewise four [points].
First, no person;
second, no phenomena; third, the exhaustion of all characteristics.
Fourth, the manifestation of principle:
herein, at the beginning and throughout, there is only the cessation of the former and the arising of the latter;
in this uninterrupted flow, ultimately there is no person.
From this to that, within the phenomena of arising and ceasing, there is ultimately no person.
Therefore, the Treatise says:
"In all worldly dharmas, there is no person within the causes and effects of dharmas."
This is what is meant by that.
Regarding the "two non-dharmas":
these are dharmas subject to arising and ceasing.
Because the subsequent arises depending on the preceding, the subsequent lacks intrinsic nature and lacks substantiality.
Furthermore, it cannot come from the preceding moment;
because the subsequent turns its back upon the preceding, it is not the preceding.
Furthermore, this [subsequent thought] does not come from the preceding thought,
because the preceding one has already ceased and perished; thus,
there is no dharma that can arrive.
Because a subsequent thought can induce what follows it,
its essence is not subsumed within that subsequent state;
thus, this [thought] likewise cannot reach the subsequent state.
Therefore, the preceding thought has no dharma that can go to the succeeding thought,
and the succeeding thought has no dharma that can come from the preceding thought;
it is only through the power of dependent origination that there appears to be a continuity.
In reality, there is not a single dharma that goes from here to there;
therefore, the treatise says:
"It is only from empty dharmas that empty dharmas arise."
This is what is meant by that.
Regarding the exhaustion of the three characteristics:
one contemplates this phenomenon as having already ceased in the past.
The future has no intrinsic nature because it has not yet arrived;
the present has no intrinsic nature because it cannot abide by itself.
Furthermore, upon reflection, the preceding thought-moment has already passed away, and thus there is no coming.
Because it does not reach the subsequent moment, there is no "going"; because it perishes as soon as the present moment arises, it cannot remain.
Therefore, these characteristics of phenomena are never exhausted.
Furthermore, upon careful reflection, one sees that the present phenomenon is not separate from the past and the future.
Because there is no separate entity apart from the beginning and the end.

First, one causes the recognition of deluded thoughts.

it is simply a single thought reaching the state of no-thought—
that very thought which acts as the subjective perceiver.
Furthermore, it is because there are no characteristics that do not accord with what is contemplated,
and because the characteristics of this and that, as well as their respective locations, are immediately empty,

Since one now knows that the reality of phenomena is thus,
all previous perceptions of distinctions between self and others, or between phenomena as right and wrong,
are entirely the conceptual constructions and deluded imaginings of a distracted consciousness.
In reality, nothing exists at all.
One should lament one's own perversion and bring all deluded thoughts to rest.
Furthermore, one should reflect as follows:
This very deluded thought pursues its own deluded objects;
these two, however, are eternally non-existent in the present.

The arising from the mind’s characteristics and the characteristics produced by the mind are in harmony;

Question: If that is so, then it would suffice for this single door to be without mindfulness;

Answer: If one does not investigate that meaning as previously described, [the understanding will not be complete].

Because they cannot bring about benefit or advantage.
As a verse in a sutra says:
"A hundred thousand monks who are like mute sheep."
If one cultivates meditative concentration without wisdom,
even for hundreds of thousands of eons,
not a single person will attain nirvana.
A person of keen faculties and wisdom can listen to the Dharma and expound the Dharma;
by concentrating their mindfulness for even a brief moment, they may attain realization.
The methods for swiftly attaining nirvana, as well as the demonic activities (*māra-karman*) within contemplation and other aspects such as the benefits of contemplation,
are all explained in detail elsewhere.

Like the interlacing net of Indra,
or like celestial jewels reflecting one another,
they are perfectly interfused, sovereign, inexhaustible, and beyond naming.

3. The Gate of the Dual Manifestation of the Nature of Conditions;

First, regarding the Gate of the Mutual Dependence of the Characteristics of Dependent Origination:
Within this, there are three gates: first,
the gate of the mutual difference of conditions,
which refers to their distinct natures.
2. The gate of mutual correspondence among conditions;
this is the aspect of identical substance.
3. The gate of unimpeded response to diversity.
This immediately provides a dual analysis of their similarities and differences.
Within these three gates, there are three meanings for each:
first, the meaning of mutual support and the presence or absence of power.
By this, they attain mutual interpenetration.
Second, regarding the meaning of the essence being both with and without substance through mutual negation and sublation,
by this, they attain mutual identity.
The third is the meaning of the simultaneous fusion of essence and function, and existence and non-existence;
by means of this, one immediately enters simultaneous mastery.
First is the gate of the mutual difference of dependent origination.
This means that within the inexhaustible great dependent origination,
the essence and function of each respective condition are distinct and do not intermingle; therefore, they are said to be "different."
Regarding the meaning of "support" (āśraya):
first, one can support many;
because one possesses power, it is therefore able to encompass many.
Because many depend upon one, the many lack power;
therefore, they merge into the one.
This one, moreover, is not such that it cannot accommodate the many.
Because there is nothing that cannot be sustained,
there is nothing that does not enter into the one;
because there is nothing that cannot rely upon the one.
Just as it is when many rely upon a single support,
so too is it when one relies upon many supports; therefore,
there is likewise no multiplicity that is not subsumed within the one.
Furthermore, there is not even one [object] that is not included within the many.
Therefore, by virtue of viewing the many through a single perspective, and because of the presence or absence of power based on the support,
one is able to encompass and enter [the objects] without obstruction.
Because there is much expectation toward a single [object] that has a basis and support, and because the weak power becomes full power,
one is able to enter and gather [them],
and there is likewise no obstruction.
The two phrases "both existing" and "both vanishing" are mutually unimpeded;
this should also be understood by analogy.
The principle of mutual inclusion is hereby concluded.
Second, regarding the mutual sublation of the nature and the lack of nature of conditions:
many conditions, being devoid of intrinsic nature, together constitute a single effect;
therefore, the many are identical to the one.
Because a single existent entity can encompass many,
and because the absence of multiplicity is inherently identical [to that unity],
there is no "one" that is not manifold.
Nor is there a multiplicity that is not one.
A single nature constitutes the many;
when the one is empty, the many are likewise so.
Therefore, one perspective encompasses many,
because it includes both that which has an intrinsic nature and that which lacks one;
thus, it can subsume others within itself.
Abandoning the self to identify with others,
there is no obstruction. Regarding the many in relation to the one, whether they exist or not, they possess both substantiality and non-substantiality.
Furthermore, one can set aside oneself to identify with others and embrace others as oneself;
there is no obstruction in identifying others as oneself and identifying oneself as others.
It is not that "other" is identical to "self," nor that "self" is identical to "other.
These two phrases are unimpeded, perfectly interfused, and sovereign;
this can be seen through reflection.
The section on the meaning of mutual identity is concluded.
Regarding the third gate, the "Double Fusion of Essence and Function through Being and Non-being," there are six propositions.
The first is: because the essence is non-existent, there is no function.
When the entire substance is entirely function, there is only function and no substance;
this is because there is only mutual penetration and non-substantiality.
Second, by means of...
Because there is no function that is not the essence, all functions return to the essence;
thus, there is only essence without function,
where there is merely mutual identity of phenomena but no mutual penetration of them.
The essence of the Three Refuges does not obstruct its function,
and the essence that fully embodies the function does not lose its essence.
Therefore, essence and function coexist without mutual obstruction.
It is both entry and identity;
there is no obstruction, as all is fused in sovereign freedom.
The substance of the fourfold total function is itself obliterated.
When the function of the whole is devoid of function,
then essence and function mutually penetrate and form and substance are both negated;
thus one enters the single source, where all is perfectly interfused in a single flavor.
The fifth unifies the preceding four phrases;
they share a single dependent origination, existing together without obstruction.
The sixth subsumes the preceding five phrases, transcending all dependence and departing from verbal expression.
One should set aside preconceptions and contemplate according to principle.
This concludes the section on the gate of the distinct entities of dependent origination.
Second is the gate of the mutual correspondence of conditions:
This means that among the various conditions, because a single condition must correspond to multiple conditions,
each one constitutes a whole for those many;
therefore, this one possesses many ones.
However, although this "many-ones" arises from the original "one," it exists as such because it must depend on many conditions;
nevertheless, it is non-different in essence from the original one.
Therefore, this is called the "Gate of Identical Substance" (*tongti men*).
Regarding "relying upon, supporting, and containing":
it means that this single fundamental [substance] possesses the power to support those many individual unities.
Therefore, the single [entity] at the root can contain those many ones;
since the many ones lack power and depend upon the single entity at the root,
the many ones enter into that single entity at the root.
This is precisely the fundamental unity that allows for the inclusion of all multiplicities,
and it is also the case that no multiplicity fails to enter into this fundamental unity;
just as the fundamental unity possesses the power to sustain them.
Since it is possible for many to rely on one who lacks power,
so too is it possible for many to be sustained by one who possesses power.
The capacity to enter [the one] based on the powerlessness of the original one is likewise so;
this is precisely that which does not exclude the many ones within the original one.
There is nothing that does not enter into the fundamental unity of the many and the one;
this is precisely because, by virtue of the fundamental unity of the one looking toward the many and the one,
there is that which maintains and that which depends, and that which possesses power and that which lacks power.
It is able to contain and enter [all things] without obstruction.
For the most part, it views the root as one;
it has both dependence and support, and thus possesses both powerlessness and power.
It can both enter and contain, and yet there is no obstruction;
existence and cessation coexist and are simultaneously extinguished—these two phrases are without hindrance.
One should likewise reflect upon this accordingly.
The section on the meaning of inclusion within the gate of identical substance is concluded.
Second, regarding the mutual negation of existence and non-existence:
this refers to the absence of self-nature in both the many and the one.
The "one-as-the-source" constitutes the many-ones;
its entire substance is precisely this source-one.
Thus, the source-one possesses a substantial body capable of encompassing the many-ones.
Because many and one are essentially non-substantial and fused within the fundamental unity,
there is no fundamental unity that does not encompass the many and one,
nor is there any many and one that is not identical with the fundamental unity.
Just as in the original case where the one has substance and the many lack it,
such that the inclusion is already thus;
so too, when the many and the one have substance, the original one lacks substance.
The same applies to inclusion.
Therefore, there is no "one" that is not included within the fundamental "one," nor is there a "one" that is not identical to the fundamental "one" within the many.
This is precisely the original "one looking toward many," because there is both that which possesses a substantial body and that which lacks one; thus,
it can subsume others into itself while discarding itself to become identical with others, resulting in non-existence.
There are obstructions.
For the most part, one should look back to the root;
furthermore, it can be understood that they are subsumed within both substantiality and non-substantiality.
Furthermore, "both encompassing and not encompassing" is itself "neither identical nor non-identical.
The two phrases—“neither encompassing nor not encompassing” and “neither identical nor non-identical”—are mutually unimpeded;
this can be seen through reflection.
The section on the meaning of mutual identity within the gate of identical substance is concluded.
Third, regarding the unimpeded entry where substance and function are both fused,
there are likewise six phrases of non-obstruction.
One may see this by reflecting upon what precedes.

This concludes the section on the gate of identical substance. Next, the third section shall simultaneously explain the gates of distinct substance and non-obstruction, as well as the gates of identical substance and distinct substance.
By means of these two gates:
Because they share the same dependent origination and are not separate from one another;
if they lacked distinct entities, then all conditions would become confused and disordered,
and thus would not constitute dependent origination.
If they were not of the same substance, the conditions would not support one another;
furthermore, they would not constitute dependent origination.
It is precisely because they are unmixed that there can be mutual support.
Therefore, since there is no difference in essence if there is not identity of essence,
and no identity of essence if there is no difference in essence,
there are likewise four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) that comprehensively distinguish this.
First, some are entirely different in their substance, yet they are mutually inclusive and simultaneous.
Second, some are identical in their entire substance, and they too are mutually inclusive and simultaneous.
This is because dharmas interpenetrate, such that each completely encompasses the others.
Third, both may be present,
because the non-obstruction between identity and difference manifests simultaneously.
Fourth, neither may be present.
Because they are both exhausted through mutual sublation, they are "neither" (ubhayābhāva).
The remaining *āyatanas* should be understood by applying this same principle accordingly.
