Chapter on the Perfect Sound. Regarding the meaning of the perfect sound, it shall be briefly analyzed through four sections:
first, the presentation of the meaning;
second, the definitive discernment.
Third, the contradictions;
fourth, the analysis and explanation.
Regarding the first [of these], there are two parts.
First, it means that the Tathāgata is able, with a single voice,
to expound all differentiated teachings;
that is to say, for those who have much greed.
Thus, they hear the Tathāgata preach the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), and so forth, up to all [other teachings]; therefore, this is called the "perfect sound" (*pariṣphuṭa-svara*).
For this reason, the *Avataṃsaka* says:
The Tathāgata, within a single utterance,
expounds an ocean of boundless sūtras.
Second, it refers to the single voice of the Tathāgata.
It is able to conform to all differentiated speech and sounds;
that is to say, each sentient being hears the Tathāgata as speaking only their own language.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
The linguistic dharmas of all sentient beings are fully expounded in a single word, without exception.
Second is the definitive analysis.
Some say that within a single vocal action, the Tathāgata produces the speech and sounds of all sentient beings.
Therefore, it causes each of those sentient beings to hear their own respective words.
It is not that the Tathāgata utters only a single sound;
rather, because the vocal karma is identical, it is called "one sound."
Because that which is uttered is manifold, it is called the "perfect sound" (saṃghuṣita). Some say,
however, that the Tathāgata utters only a single Brahma-sound.
It is called "Single Sound.
It can act as a dominant condition for sentient beings,
causing their respective understandings of what is produced to differ.
Therefore, it is called the "perfect sound.
This does not mean that the Tathāgata possesses various distinct voices.
Or, as some might say:
The Tathāgata’s sole state of quiescent liberation, which is free from signs, words, and sounds,
is called the "one voice. Yet,
due to the power of the sentient beings' receptive capacities and their karmic responses, [it appears as many voices].
Because sentient beings hear the various vocal expressions of the Tathāgata from their own perspective,
it is called the "perfect sound" (pariṣanda-ghoṣa).
This does not mean that the Tathāgata’s voice is either singular or manifold.
Question: Regarding these three preceding explanations, what are their respective gains and losses?
Answer: If one takes them up individually or in isolation, all three possess faults.
Why is this? Because the first [statement] refers only to the multiplicity [of sounds] and not to a single sound;
the second refers only to a single utterance and not to multiple sounds.

Subsequently, because there is no meaning in the sounds "only," "not," or "neither," the true meaning is that these three explanations combined constitute a single, perfect sound-meaning (*ekadhvani-artha*).
Why is this? If those many sounds were not immediately one sound,
then these would merely be many sounds and would not possess the meaning of being "perfectly round" (circular).
Because those many sounds are identical to a single sound,
their seamless fusion is called the "perfect sound" (saṃbhinnabuddhasvara).
If that single sound were not identical to all [sounds], it would not be perfect.
However, this single sound is not the Brahma-sound.
Because that single sound is itself many sounds,
its unhindered integration is called the "single Brahma-sound."
If these sounds were not immediately devoid of intrinsic nature and identical with the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi),
they would be objects of conceptual grasping and thus would not be the voice of the Tathāgata.
Because those sounds and so forth are free from volitional construction,
lack intrinsic nature, and are like echoes,
the Dharma conch constantly vibrates with wondrous sound that is eternally quiescent.
Regarding the third contradiction:
as stated in the seventy-ninth fascicle of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*,
there were times when the World-Honored One acted on behalf of the Four Heavenly Kings.
First, he spoke of the Four Noble Truths in the sacred language (āryabhāṣā).
The two kings understood it, but the other two could not.
Out of compassion and for their benefit, the World-Honored One [acted].
He spoke the Four Noble Truths using the vernacular of a frontier kingdom in South India;
among the two celestial kings, one understood while the other did not.
The World-Honored One felt compassion for them.
Furthermore, when he preached the Four Noble Truths in each of the various Mleccha languages, the Four Heavenly Kings all attained understanding. [The interlocutor] asked:
"If a single sound is understood differently by different classes of beings, [how is this possible?]"
Why do the latter two Heavenly Kings not have the same understanding?
The answer is that the treatise explains:
the dispositions (āśaya) of those Four Heavenly Kings are different.
The Buddha spoke differently in order to fulfill their intentions.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One wished to manifest his mastery in understanding all modes of speech and sound,
thereby severing their doubts.
Furthermore, there are those to be converted who receive transformation by relying on the Buddha’s unchanging form and speech;
and there are those to be converted who receive transformation by relying on the Buddha’s transformed form and speech.
Those who are transformed by relying on the Buddha’s unchanging forms and speech would be unable to understand if he were to transform his forms and speech to preach the Dharma for them.
As it is said: when the Buddha was in the kingdom of Magadha, he walked twelve yojanas to convert the pond-dweller Kaṇṭaka;
seventy thousand sentient beings all attained the vision of the Truth (dṛṣṭasatya), and so forth.
Those who are transformed and guided by means of the Buddha’s manifested forms and speech would be unable to understand if he were to preach the Dharma without manifesting such forms and speech.
Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke in three ways when preaching the Dharma for the Four Heavenly Kings.
Following the three previous explanations, the underlying principles are applicable;
in each case, it is because the inclinations of sentient beings for whom they should hear the teaching differ.
Therefore, there is no contradiction.
Regarding the fourth section, the analysis and explanation, there are two parts.
The first clarifies the boundaries.
The second [section] reveals the benefits.
Regarding the first [of these], a single utterance of the Buddha’s voice pervades all things—
meaning all places, all times, and all dharmas.
Those whose faculties are mature hear it from afar;
those whose faculties are not yet mature do not hear it even when it is near.
Thus, it is said that [the teaching] pervades all places.
As stated in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, Maudgalyāyana perceived sounds from an extreme distance as if they were near.
Second, it pervades all time; that is, this perfect voice continues without ceasing throughout the limits of the future.
Third, it pervades all phenomena;
there is not a single phenomenon that has not been proclaimed by the Perfect Sound.
Fourth, it pervades all sentient beings.
This means that there is no faculty or capacity whatsoever that this perfect sound does not awaken.
If that is so, why was Śāriputra in the assembly as if deaf and did not hear it?
This explanation does not mean that the perfect voice can reach the place where it is heard;
rather, it is called "pervasive" because it can also reach places where it is not heard.
Question: If this [phoneme] were universal, how could it constitute the articulated expression of speech through its various inflections?
If that were so, what would be the fault?
Both positions are flawed.
Why? Because if this were the case, it would result in the loss of the musical melody due to its being equal and pervasive.
If it were to exist in a distorted manner, it would not be uniform or pervasive.
Now, to explain: if it were to lose its tonal curves due to being uniform and pervasive, it would be a sphere rather than sound.
If it were due to being bent that it failed to be equal and pervasive,
then this sound would not be spherical;
however, in the present case, it is neither impaired by its curvature nor does it fail to be equal and pervasive.
That which is immovable, all-pervasive, and differentiated by its melodic resonance is called the Tathāgata’s perfect voice.
It is not an object of conceptualization or deliberation by the mind and consciousness.
Second, regarding the two benefits:
According to the Hīnayāna, the speech and sounds of the Tathāgata do not necessarily all possess benefit.
For example, when the Buddha asked Ānanda about the rain falling from the heavens and so forth,
such instances are not subsumed under the sound of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).
If, within the Mahāyāna and other [teachings],
all the conventional sounds and speech uttered by the Tathāgata invariably bring about great benefit, then...
Just as when the Buddha enters a city, he utters the sound of begging for alms so that all within the city may hear it together and collectively obtain benefit.
As the Sūtra says:
The sounds, speech, dignified demeanor, and movements of all Buddhas are none other than Buddha-works.
Regarding the chapter on the Dharma-body, the meaning of the Dharma-body is analyzed through four gates.
First, as for the explanation of the name:
The Dharma has the meaning of being a guide and support;
the body has the meaning of being a basis.
Thus, the Dharma constitutes the body.
It is also called the *svabhāvakāya* (Self-nature Body).
Regarding its two essential natures, there are briefly ten types.
First, according to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*:
It has only the true suchness (tathatā), the pure dharma-dhātu, as its nature;
the other four wisdoms and so forth all belong to the recompense and transformation bodies.
Second, it may refer exclusively to wisdom,
as in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* by Asvabhāva,
which holds that the dharmakāya consists of stainless and unimpeded wisdom.
This refers to being free from the two obstacles.
Various virtuous commentators explain that this is based on the principle of subsuming the objects within the mind, which is termed the *dharmakāya*.
It is not that the Dharmakāya is wisdom and not principle;
for if all dharmas are now explained as being identical with True Suchness (tathatā),
how much more so this true wisdom— which could it possibly not be such?
Since this is already the case, how can it encompass objects?
The third [category] is both wisdom and object.
As the *She dasheng lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) of the Liang dynasty states:
Only suchness and the wisdom of suchness remain alone;
this is called the Dharmakāya.
Here, both the four objects and the wisdom are simultaneously extinguished.
The Sūtra states:
"The Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata is neither mind nor object.
These four preceding lines together constitute the unimpeded Dharmakāya.
According with these explanations, one attains all six [aspects].
Beyond this, the five phrases—both general and specific—are mutually integrated, mutually negated, and thus extinguished;
these five teachings are universally non-reliant, constituting the Dharmakāya.
The above has distinguished [the stages] solely by way of object and wisdom;
the seventh stage universally encompasses the five factors,
as well as the merits of spiritual practice such as compassion and the vow.
There is nothing that is not subsumed within this dharmakāya,
because the merits produced through cultivation necessarily realize the principle.
Their seamless integration and non-obstruction are as previously explained regarding wisdom.
The eightfold merit of manifesting physical forms through emanation is all encompassed within this Dharma-body,
for there is nothing that is not subsumed therein; thus,
the thirty-two marks and so forth mentioned in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* are included.
All are subsumed within the Dharmakāya; this comprises three meanings:
first, because their characteristics are identical to Suchness (tathatā), they return to the Dharmakāya of Principle;
second, because they are manifested by wisdom, they belong to the Dharmakāya of Wisdom.
Third, these three are mutually concurrent dharmas of merit;
therefore, it is called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Ninth, because it universally encompasses all three worlds.
Because sentient beings and the vessel-world are none other than the Buddha;
because one Great Dharmakāya possesses the ten Buddhas;
and because the three bodies and so forth are all contained herein.
Because it is subsumed within the wisdom of perfect enlightenment,
the ten [qualities] are collectively treated as one summary phrase;
this is called the meaning of the Tathāgata’s unimpeded and sovereign Dharma-body.
There are four causes for manifestation.
The first is the revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*),
because it illuminates and manifests the *tathatā* (suchness) that has existed inherently from the beginning.
Second is the cause of production,
because it brings about the arising of superior qualities through cultivation.
Third is the cause of the unimpeded realization of non-arising.
Because the characteristic of arising and the two fruits are not distinct.
Fourth, taking these supreme virtues collectively as the causal basis (*āśraya-hetu*),
one realizes the fruit of manifesting the seal according to the capacity [of the practitioner].
Regarding the four functional activities, there are likewise four.
First, this principle-dharmakāya serves as the object of awakening for all contemplative wisdoms.
The Sūtra states:
"Because the Dharma-body preaches the Dharma and bestows its meaning;
and second, because it gives rise to the superior karmic functions of the Reward and Transformation bodies to benefit sentient beings."
Third, it manifests as trees and so forth through the subtle gathering of transformations;
fourth, it pervades all realms of sensory objects, even down to the tip of a hair,
possessing a layered, sovereign, and unimpeded functional activity.
Chapter Ten on the Ten Ages. The meaning of the ten ages is presented in two sections.
First, regarding their establishment:
for example, when a phenomenon within the past age has not yet ceased.
These are designated as past and present.
Furthermore, in relation to the past, that past is called the "past-of-the-past.
In relation to the present, this [present] is yet to come.
Therefore, the present is designated as past and future.
This single set exists entirely within the past;
furthermore, once that has ceased, the present dharma arises.
That which has not yet ceased is called "present";
because it is contrasted with that past which has already perished and is non-existent, it is designated as "present-past."
That which is expected in the future is yet non-existent;
therefore, it is called "present and future.
These three [aspects] are all simultaneously present in the present.
Furthermore, when those dharmas have ceased, future dharmas arise;
while they have not yet ceased, they are called "future-present.
In relation to that present which has already ceased, they are non-existent.
Therefore, it is called "future-past.
Furthermore, because it has not yet arisen even in relation to the future,
it is called "future-future."
These three [categories] are all present together in the future.
Among these nine, there are three each;
in the present there are six, while in the past and future they are entirely absent.
Question: If one establishes three time periods for each of the past and the future,
then since the past and future are each infinite,
these three time periods would also be infinite.
Why are nine [categories] taught instead of merely three?
Answer: Even if one were to establish further categories regarding the past and future, they would not differ from the preceding framework; therefore, there are only nine.
Furthermore, these nine periods of time are collectively a single thought-moment,
yet the nine periods remain distinct.
Thus, by combining the general and the particular, they are discussed as the ten periods of time.
Regarding the second [section], the mutual inclusion of characteristics, there are two gates:
first, the identity of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-samāveśa*), and second, the interpenetration of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-praveśa*). These two are established by virtue of two meanings.
First, the meaning of mutual dependence through conditions;
second, the meaning of the interpenetration of the dharma-nature.
Regarding the first, the meaning of mutual dependence through conditions:
Furthermore, take for example past and present phenomena:
while they have not yet passed away, they are themselves the present.
From the perspective of the present as the present, [they are so designated].
This is precisely the past within the present;
therefore, that dharma is both present and past.
Because the perspectives from which they are viewed differ, there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, that which is present is a present phenomenon;
it is present because it has not yet passed away.
This is in relation to the past and the present.
It is the future of the past; furthermore,
when viewed from the perspective of the future and the present,
it is again the past of the future.
Therefore, those dharmas are both present and past and future.
Furthermore, future and present dharmas are also both present and future.
This can be seen by comparison.
Furthermore, among these nine [types of mind],
those belonging to the three time periods and the present do not necessarily arise simultaneously.
Sixth, the past and future do not coexist either. There are two [possibilities]:
first, the present;
second, the past and future.
These three attainments (samāpatti) are acquired simultaneously;
therefore, among the nine [attainments], some are latent and some are manifest according to their respective conditions,
because they are both simultaneous and non-simultaneous.
Furthermore, within the context of coexistence, because the past of the past does not exist,
it allows for the existence of past and present phenomena. Why is this so?
If that [past] did not exist, this [present] would not exist;
furthermore, because the past and present do exist,
it follows that the past must have been non-existent [in the future].
This is because, if this were not present, that would cease to exist;
furthermore, it is by virtue of the existence of the past and the present that the past and the future are rendered non-existent.
Because that has not yet ceased, this does not yet exist;
furthermore, because the past and future do not exist by virtue of this [present],
that [past] and the present are established as existing.
Because this exists, that has already ceased; therefore, by virtue of this, that does not yet exist, since it has not yet ceased.
Furthermore, because the past is non-existent as a past [entity].
This would entail that the past and future do not exist.
That is to say: if those [past and future] were not non-existent, this present could not be established as existent;
if the present were not established as existent, this future could not be established as non-existent.
Therefore, this [present] does not exist through a successive dependence on that [past],
because that [past] is non-existent. Furthermore, because the past and future are non-existent,
it causes the past of the past to be non-existent as well.

and the sense of the distinction between the characteristics of the rabbit.
Because they are combined into a single limit, they are not different.
This is a case of the fundamental following the derivative;
it clarifies their non-difference by way of the derivative.
Second, because the meaning of the cloth abiding in its own position and the meaning of the body of the rabbit being empty are combined into a single limit, they are not different.
This is returning the branches to the root to clarify that they are not different from the root;
third, it is the root to which the branches are subsumed and the branches from which the root is derived.
Because these two are fused as a pair, unimpeded, and coexistent, they are non-different.
This is the non-differentiation in which both the root and the branches coexist without impediment.
Fourth, [it concerns] the branches that are subsumed back into the root.
Furthermore, it is not different from the root that follows what is subsumed;
since these two are simultaneously extinguished, they are non-different.
This is the equality of the simultaneous extinction of both root and branch, which is non-differentiation.
Regarding the second point, that they do not have the same meaning, there are likewise four propositions.
First, the sense of the cloth remaining in its own position is distinguished from the characteristics upon the rabbit.

Because these two are contradictory, they are not one; they are mutually opposed and not identical. The sense that a rabbit is established upon a cloth and the sense that the essence of the rabbit is empty—these two are mutually destructive, and therefore they are not one.
Third, because those [states] are mutually opposed and these [states] are mutually harmful,
these two positions are distinct and therefore not one.
That is to say, "opposition" means that each is turned away from the other, abandoning one another and remaining at a vast distance.
Mutual harm constitutes enmity, yet they are intimately devouring one another;
therefore, the near and the far are not one.
Fourth, through extreme mutual harm, they vanish and yet do not vanish.
Because they do not exist due to their extreme mutual non-existence,
this meaning of "not being extinguished" and "not existing" is not one;
this refers to the multiplicity of formation and destruction.
Furthermore, these four are not identical to the aforementioned four, yet they are also not different from them,
because their meanings do not overlap. Moreover,
the aforementioned four are not different from these four, yet these four are not identical to them.
Furthermore, because it does not differ from the principle that pervades all,
if one takes it through the perspective of non-difference,
all perspectives will be perfectly harmonized.
If one were to grasp [these matters] through a non-uniform approach,
the various meanings would be in extreme conflict;
yet that which is extremely contradictory is also extremely harmonious.
This is the dharma of non-obstruction.
Regarding the second point, which explains it in terms of dharmas:
the headcloth is a metaphor for *tathatā* (suchness) and the *tathāgatagarbha* (womb of the Tathāgata).
The analogy of the rabbit represents the birth and death of sentient beings and so forth;
it is neither identical nor different, and there are also ten gates [of analysis].
One may understand this by reflecting upon the analogy accordingly.
Furthermore, the rabbit is born and dies simultaneously without obstruction;
the headband is hidden and revealed simultaneously without obstruction.
Thus, birth and death, concealment and manifestation, and the interweaving of the adverse and the favorable are entangled together.
The various gates [of the preceding section] are all to be understood by applying the same contemplation as before; they may be subsumed accordingly.
Second, regarding the clarification of the meaning, there are four gates. The first is the opening and closing [of the gates].
2. Identity and difference;
3. characteristics are suchness;
4. characteristics abide.
Regarding the initial opening and closing:
first there is the opening, followed by the closing.
As for the opening, within the conventional truth of dependent origination (*saṃvṛti-satya pratītyasamutpāda*), there are four meanings.
First, the meaning of the conditions possessing power;
second, the meaning of their lacking power;
third, the meaning of the absence of intrinsic nature.
The meaning established by the four factors.
Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there are likewise four meanings.
First, the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Second, the meaning of non-emptiness;
third, the meaning of support;
fourth, the meaning of the exhaustion of phenomena.
There are three ways of unification:
first, unifying with the conventional;
second, unifying with the ultimate.
The third [section] combines with the second.
Regarding the first, there are three parts.
The first is based on function.
This means that there is no duality between having power and lacking power.
Second, regarding their essence:
it means that there is no duality between existence and non-existence.
The three non-obstructions refer to the non-duality of essence and function, which is solely the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Those that accord with the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) are likewise three.
First, regarding function:
this means that the conventional is established based on the foundational support; thus, the conventional is completely sublated, leaving no duality.
Second, regarding essence: it is because emptiness and non-emptiness are non-dual.
The three non-obstructions mean that essence and function are non-dual.
Regarding the synthesis of the three into two, there are four gates; the first is the gate of the arousal of function.
This refers to the meaning of being the support within the ultimate truth,
which is non-dual with the meaning of possessing power within the conventional truth.
Second, this is according to the gate of the sublation of characteristics.
This means that within the ultimate truth, the conventional is exhausted;
and within the conventional, there is no duality with respect to powerlessness.
Third, this is according to the gate of manifesting reality.
This refers to the meaning of non-emptiness within the ultimate truth,
which is non-dual with the meaning of the absence of intrinsic nature within conventional truth.
Fourth is the gate of accomplishing activities.
This means that the meaning of emptiness within the ultimate truth and the meaning of the existence of phenomena within the conventional truth are non-dual.
The section on the gates of opening and closing is concluded.
Regarding the gate of the identity and non-identity of principle and phenomena: herein, principle and phenomena are both identical and not identical.
There are four propositions for each regarding unimpeded interpenetration.
First, concerning the four propositions that [the parts] are not identical with the whole:
first, the individual phenomena do not mutually coincide.
Because the objects of conditions are obstructed by their characteristics,
the principles of these two pairs of things do not coincide;
this is because they are not two.
Third, principle and phenomena do not coincide,
because principle is quiescent and not active.
Fourth, phenomena and principle do not coincide.
Because movement by means of phenomena is not quiescence.
Regarding the four propositions within the identity of the two aspects:
first, phenomena are identical to principle.
Because dependent origination lacks intrinsic nature,
principle is identical to phenomena;
for phenomena are established through principle following conditions.
Third, the principle and the characteristic of the two matters are mutually identical,
because by means of the provisional expression one realizes the reality.
Fourth, the two matters themselves are mutually identical.
Because the phenomena that are themselves the principle are not distinct from the principle, phenomena are thus unimpeded, being identical to the principle. Section Eight:
The Gate of the Mind and Objects of Reality and Delusion. Regarding the mind and objects of reality and delusion, there are generally four propositions.
First, regarding the mind and its objects from the perspective of emotional attachment:
"objects" refers to the mutual opposition between emptiness and existence,
because these two characteristics are maintained.
"Mind" refers to the fact that the two views are not destroyed because they are deluded sentiments;
alternatively, there is a commonality of emptiness regarding the objects,
as both are equally grasped [as real].
The same applies to the mind,
as both are equally false perceptions.
Second, regarding phenomena, there are likewise the mind and its objects.
The objective realm refers to the non-duality of emptiness and existence,
because both are mutually integrated.
The mind refers to the transcendence of dualistic views.
Because they are seen as non-dual;
or because existence and emptiness are contradictory within the object,
since the latter completely supersedes the former.
There are also two [aspects] regarding the mind:
namely, because the nature of one part does not differ from that of the other parts as they are perceived.
Thirdly, this is explained by conforming the subjective sentiment to the objective phenomenon.

This means that regarding the object, both existence and non-existence are equally present from the perspective of conventional cognition (*saṃvṛti-satya*). From the perspective of ultimate reasoning (*yukti*), both existence and non-existence are absent; thus, the non-dual is of a single nature.
Alternatively, they may also be contradictory, because each completely negates the other.
"Mind" refers to the false grasping that exists within the emotional realm;
it is because of this clinging mind that one may also infer through reasoning that [the object] is non-existent, by means of analyzing the mind that perceives existence.
Fourth, explaining from the perspective of the subjective mind according to the Dharma:
as for the object, both existence and non-existence are logically established;
yet both existence and non-existence are absent from the perspective of the mind. Thus, the non-duality [of existence and non-existence] constitutes a single nature.
Alternatively, it may also be contradictory,
because it completely supersedes [the former].
"Mind" refers to the seeing of principle, for there is wisdom therein.
This is because there is no basis for compassion regarding perceived objects.
Alternatively, it is because the non-dual mind is the one mind.
Among these four preceding gates:
Regarding each object, there are four propositions;
regarding each mind, there are likewise four propositions.
In total, there are thirty-two propositions.
Reflect upon this accordingly. 9.
The Integration of the Transformer and the Transformed into Ten Gates. Ninth: The Integration of the Arising and Interpenetration of All Buddhas and Sentient Beings consists of ten gates in total.
First is the gate of stages.
The Buddha has two meanings:
first, the equality of the Dharma-body.
Second, the distinction between the retributive and transformation [bodies].
These two belong to the category of the Buddha as the transformer;
sentient beings likewise possess these two meanings.
First is the *tathāgatagarbha* as the basis;
second is the deluded defilements that depend upon it.
These two constitute the gateway for those sentient beings to be transformed.
Second is the gate of principle and phenomena.
This is because the Buddha’s Dharma-body and the Tathāgatagarbha of sentient beings are non-dual in nature.
This is the Dharma-gate of Principle.
Because the Buddha’s retributive and transformational bodies and the deluded defilements of sentient beings are mutually dependent,
this is the Dharma-gate of Phenomena.
Third, because the Dharma-body is not different from the Tathāgatagarbha,
while the Reward-body and Transformation-body manifest in dependence upon the defiled vessel;
therefore, they are all collectively categorized under the category of sentient beings.
Fourth, because the Tathāgatagarbha is not different from the Dharmakāya,
and because false defilements are what are overturned by the Saṃbhogakāya and Nirmāṇakāya,
it follows that all of these belong to the Buddha-vehicle.
Fifth, because phenomena are empty and lack intrinsic substance,
and because the nature of reality is unchanging,
there is only the single gateway of principle.
Sixth, because principle follows conditions and because there is no phenomenon that does not exist,
there is only the single gate of phenomena.
Seventh, because the retributive and transformational [bodies] externally encompass deluded defilement while internally encompassing the rational nature,

they belong exclusively to the gate of retribution and transformation. Eighth, because deluded defilement can manifest the retributive and transformational [bodies], it is further internally encompassed by true reality.
9. Only the gate of false defilement.
10. The gate of simultaneous existence, wherein all the aforementioned meanings manifest without obstruction;
the gate of harmonious fusion and equality, wherein all the aforementioned meanings are interfused and equal.
This is the gate of mutual extinction.
These ten gates should be understood by analogy with the six characteristics. Gate Ten:
The Gate of Expedient Means for Entering the Path. Regarding the expedient means for entering the path, there must be three essential elements that serve as the causal conditions for entry.
First, identifying the affliction;
second, discerning the object;
third, determining the wisdom.
The beginning and middle have two [aspects]:
first, the coarse, which refers to seeking fame, profit, and so forth;
second, the subtle, which refers to maintaining views and adhering to principles, and so forth.
Second, regarding the exclusion of objects, there are two parts.
First, as for the object:
it refers to objects that are sentient or non-sentient, located at the boundaries, and so forth.
The second, the true realm, has two aspects.
First is the realm of the Three Vehicles,
which refers to the non-dual, harmonious integration of emptiness and existence, and so forth.
Second, the object of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*),
which refers to the common, exhaustive dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) characterized by the perfection of qualities, its circular integration (*yuanrong*), and so forth. Third,
within meditative concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā*), there are likewise two [aspects].
First, "understanding" (adhimukti) refers to that which can generate correct understanding;
specifically, it is the understanding that recognizes the distinction between understanding (*jñāna*) and practice (*pratipatti*).
Second, "practice" (*pratipatti*) refers to acting in accordance with what has been understood.
Because understanding cannot reach [the ultimate],
there is the non-conceptual mind’s practice that accords with phenomena, such as deluded sentiments;
furthermore, this practice is established based on understanding.
Furthermore, when practice manifests before one, that understanding must necessarily be severed.
Moreover, regarding the object,
one should distinguish it by using the three types of emptiness to unsettle the mind.
By means of practice, one distinguishes between them through non-conceptual wisdom;
thus its meaning becomes evident.
Furthermore, the skillful means for entering the Path are briefly set forth in four gates.
1. The gate of repentance for removing past obstacles;
2. The gate of generating the bodhicitta;
3. The gate of receiving the bodhisattva precepts.
Fourth is the gate of cultivating sublime practices.
There are two paths for cultivating sublime practices:
first, the beginning; second, the end.
In the beginning and middle, there are three gates:
first, the gate of relinquishing conditions;
second, the gate of following conditions.
The third is the gate of practice.
Within its beginning, there are six stages.
The first is the relinquishing of unwholesome karma.
Second, abandoning relatives and kin:
if one leaves the household life, one abandons disciples and those who are one's natural kinsmen.
Third, abandoning fame and gain.
Fourth, relinquishing body and life;
fifth, relinquishing mental conceptions;
sixth, relinquishing.
This equanimity causes the severance of subject and object, as there is no longer any basis for reliance.
Second, regarding the gate of following conditions,
there are four levels.
First, one should follow the previous six matters and maintain the mind so that it remains unstained.
Second, regarding all objects capable of stirring the emotions— even those as slight as the most minute—
one should be aware of them and not accept them, ensuring there is not even the slightest defilement.
Third, regarding all adverse conditions—
even enemies who would deprive one of life—
one should maintain a joyful mind and endure them with patience.
Fourth, in all actions one performs, one remains far removed from artifice, hypocrisy, and deceit,
not allowing even a single thought-moment of them to arise.
Third is the gate of accomplishing practice.
First, the practice of each of the six pāramitās, and so forth;
second, the practice of each of the four immeasurables, and so forth;
third, the practice of each of the thirty great vows, and so forth.
There are two aspects of aspiration and practice:
first, to exert effort so that all practices not yet initiated may be brought forth;
second, to maintain those already initiated so that they do not regress.
All of these arise from the power of vows, which is precisely the penetration of the practice of the Dharma.
Second, regarding the conclusion, there are also three gates.
First is the gate of relinquishment.
This is precisely the practice of cessation.
One contemplates that all phenomena are equal and of a single mark,
such that all conditions are severed, and so forth.
The second, the gate of following conditions, refers to contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
It involves giving rise to great compassion, great vows, and other such practices within the midst of phenomena, and so forth.
The third is the gate of accomplishing practice.
Thus, calming and insight are practiced together in a state of dual fusion and non-obstruction,
achieving the practice of non-abiding.
The realms of the ultimate and the conventional are not distinct, and the minds of compassion and wisdom are not separate.
Furthermore, this object is not distinct [from the subject].
Moreover, it clarifies that the bodhisattva dwells in the practice of non-dwelling;
this is explained through two gates.
First, opening; second, closing.
Within opening, there are also two:
first, non-abiding.
The subsequent explanation of abiding and non-abiding also has two aspects:
first, not abiding in saṃsāra;
second, not abiding in nirvāṇa.
In the beginning and the middle, there are also two [reasons]:
first, because one sees the faults and afflictions of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one cannot abide therein;
second, because one sees that birth and death are fundamentally empty, there is nothing in which to abide.
Second, non-abiding in nirvāṇa is also twofold.
First, because one sees that nirvāṇa is inherently present from the beginning,
one does not wait for it to abide.
Second, because it is not distinct from saṃsāra, one does not abide;
furthermore, because wisdom and principle are non-dual and subject and object are severed, there is no one who can abide.
Second, the explanation of abiding also has two parts.
First, regarding those who abide in saṃsāra, there are also two aspects.
The first is that they give rise to great compassion because they perceive its defects.
One dwells [in this state] for the purpose of eliminating the fetters (*paryavasthāna*).
Furthermore, there are two reasons: first, one dwells because one sees emptiness and thus is not afraid;
second, one dwells because one perceives faults and consequently develops revulsion.
Second, seeing emptiness, one abides in nirvāṇa;
this is precisely being constantly within saṃsāra while eternally abiding in nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, there are two types of those who abide in nirvāṇa.
First, he abides because he constantly realizes the principle;
second, he abides because he constantly transforms sentient beings,
for those beings to be transformed are themselves nirvana.
The second combination consists of four parts.
First, because birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are non-dual,
there is no partial dwelling.
Therefore, it is called "non-abiding.
Furthermore, because one abides precisely in this state of non-duality,
it is also called "abiding."
Regarding the two types of practice— dwelling and non-dwelling—
it is precisely because one takes non-dwelling as dwelling and dwelling as non-dwelling that there is only the single practice of non-conceptuality.
Therefore, there is no duality.
Regarding the two gates of the threefold union and the sphere of practice:
because the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) transcends the distinction between subject and object.
Because the equal nature of phenomena (dharmatā) has but a single flavor,
there is no distinction between object and practice.
These four, combined with the preceding opening and this present section, constitute a non-dual and undifferentiated gateway to the Dharma that is solely unimpeded.
Therefore, it is unimpeded in its opening yet eternally closed;
it is not destroyed in its closing yet eternally open, because these two characteristics are non-dual.
Thus, it is beyond the reach of verbal expression.
If further analyzed by way of numerical categories, there are four sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first is: abiding neither in saṃsāra nor in nirvāṇa alone.
Second, those who abide only in non-abiding nirvana are also such;
third, those who abide in neither are also such;
fourth, those who abide in neither [of these two] are also such.
The second case—dwelling in only one—also consists of four permutations;
reflect upon them by reversing the above.
The third case—dwelling in saṃsāra alone and not dwelling in saṃsāra at all—is as follows.
Both "both" and "neither" are knowable.
The fourth [category] is exclusively abiding in nirvāṇa, while "exclusively not abiding in nirvāṇa" applies to both "both" and "neither.
Both "both" and "neither" are likewise exclusively so.
Regarding these sixteen gates above, each gate is attained in its entirety.
Upon attaining one, there is no need for the others;
yet the remaining gates are not thereby impaired.
Therefore, there is neither obstruction nor hindrance.
Many are simply many; one is simply one.
Contemplate this by taking up or discarding according to wisdom.
